newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Grains - Wheat futures off to slow start.
newsitem.headline: Australia Grains - Wheat futures off to slow start.

text.p: Wheat futures trading at the Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) started the week with activity limited to a A$2.00 move higher in the January contract on Monday amid light volumes.

While the futures market in Chicago ended slightly higher last week in response to "extremely oversold conditions," the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) supply and demand figures were expected to keep prices under pressure in the near term, Australia-based New England Agricultural Traders Pty Ltd said.
The USDA on Friday in its July wheat production forecast, pegged 1997 U.S. winter wheat production at 1.781 billion bushels, above an average of analysts' estimates for 1.687 billion bushels.
But the USDA also pegged total wheat production at 2.431 billion bushels, below the average analyst expectation for 2.433 billion. There are 36.74371 bushels in a tonne.

New England Agricultural noted that although the USDA raised their estimate of world wheat output to 586 million tonnes, the latest figure includes 18.5 million tonnes from Australia and 13.5 million tonnes from Argentina.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) has revised down its estimate for production for the 1997/98 wheat crop now being planted to a range of between 15 million and 16 million tonnes from 18 million tonnes.
Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd pegs the 1997/98 harvest at 17.87 million tonnes.

"At this stage, the Australian estimate looks to be two to three million tonnes too high, whilst a a reduction in acreage and poor fertiliser sales in Argentina indicate their crop will likely be one to two million tonnes smaller," it said.

"Combined with smaller crops in South Africa and India and higher demand from Asia and North Africa, this confirms our view that seasonal lows will soon be in place and the market should recover some of the ground which has been lost."
New England Agricutural said a bull market in wheat was unlikely to develop, adding that a scale up selling programme was advisable at this stage.
"With Sydney futures trading at A$172/tonne (in-store Newcastle), there seems to be some upside in Chicago already built into the price," it said.
Meanwhile, a subdued market for old crop wheat is expected to persist, with demand low.

The AWB has underlined the fact that feedgrains sorghum were key factors in the market last week on the east coast of Australia, with significant stocks still available in Queensland and New South Wales.
New England Agricutural said there has been a slight improvement in sorghum values, while barley also appears better supported.
"With no substantial rain over the growing areas recently and none forecast, we feel this trend will continue," New England Agricutural said.

Wheat shipping yards across Australia saw a reasonable level of activity, with New South Wales shipping a significant load to Pakistan, and Indonesian and Iraqi deliveries leaving Western Australia and Queensland terminals.
